en.title: The Book of De · Chapter Seventeen · Skilled in Beholding
en.原文:
善建者不拔 善抱者不脫 子孫以祭祀不絕 

修之身 亓德乃真 修之家 亓德有餘 修之鄉 亓德乃長 修之邦 亓德乃豐 修之天下 亓德乃博 

以身觀身 以家觀家 以鄉觀鄉 以邦觀邦 以天下觀天下 

吾何以知天下然茲 以此
en.字龕:
### 觀 *guān* — beholding

**字 Graph** ｜ 篆 ![觀之篆](/book-assets/hosuke-laozi-en/zhuan/%E8%A7%80.svg)

**文 Gloss** ｜ The *Shuowen*: 「諦視也。從見，雚聲。」 — "To look with full attention. From 見, seeing; 雚 as sound."

**像 Image** ｜ Not a glance, not a stare: 諦視 is the look that is steady, long, and takes everything in — the watcher's seeing, not the passerby's.

**義 Sense** ｜ Five times in this chapter the sage beholds — and never once *infers*. As the commentary reads it: the Confucian extends himself outward (推); Laozi's man holds his own De up as a mirror, and like shows itself in like. Beholding is the whole of his politics of knowing.

en.疏:
杳眇曰：

「善建者不拔，善抱者不脫」——建者植根於內，非築於外；抱者守一於心，非執物於手。內建則外物不能拔，守一以無心則永不脫。二句言德立於內，不立於外也。德充於身者，其澤自流於後嗣，故曰「子孫以祭祀不絕」。王弼本作「輟」，輟者中斷也，與帛書「絕」義同。

脩德有五等之序：由身而家，而鄉，而邦，而天下。脩之身其德乃真，脩之家其德乃餘，脩之鄉其德乃長，脩之邦其德乃豐，脩之天下其德乃博。五者相承而進，此老子由近及遠、由小徂大之義也。《大學》云「自天子以至於庶人，壹是皆以修身為本」，正與此相發明——老子先《大學》而立此格局，先秦經學內在之一致，於此可見。

然儒道於此五級之精神別焉：儒家由己推人，是「擴而充之」；道家由己及物，是「自然被之」。儒由有推有，道由無被無。故儒家近於推己，老子則言「觀」——觀者非推也，乃以己之德為鏡，照見彼德之所在。以身觀身、以家觀家、以鄉觀鄉、以邦觀邦、以天下觀天下——皆以內驗外、以近驗遠、以同類相照之法也。欲知天下，觀其一邦可驗；欲知一邦，觀其一鄉可驗；欲知一鄉，觀其一家可驗；欲知一家，觀其一身可驗。此即幾於道之說也。

尤要者，帛書作「其德乃博」，王弼易以「其德乃普」，一字之間，旨趣殊隔。博者量廣，有餘之謂；普者遍及，無遺之謂。德之流布，如江河不擇細流、大海不辭百川，自然而周遍，故老子用「博」。王弼作「普」，已近儒家「推而廣之」之義，非老子自被之旨矣。道之真義在乎「以治身為本，其緒餘以為國家」，由真以至博，其序不可紊也。

末云「吾何以知天下之然也？以此」——「此」者何？自身之德而已。知天下之亂治，不在外探，乃在內驗。身之德正則家自齊，家齊則鄉自睦，鄉睦則邦自治，邦治則天下自平。聖人不出戶以知天下，不窺牖以見天道——以身為鏡，以德為則，此老子政治認識論之極簡也。《中庸》曰「致中和，天地位焉，萬物育焉」，其此之謂乎。
en.疏英:
Yaomiao says:

"What is well planted is not pulled up; what is well held does not slip away": planting means rooting within, not building without; holding means keeping the One in the heart, not clutching a thing in the hand. Rooted within, no outer force can pull it up; keeping the One with no-heart, it never slips. The two lines say one thing: De stands inside, not outside. When De fills the body, its bounty flows of itself to the descendants. Hence "sons and grandsons keep the sacrifice unbroken." The Wang Bi recension writes 輟, "interrupted," for the silk text's 絕, "cut off": one sense.

The cultivation of De has five ranks in file: from body to house to village to state to all-under-heaven. In the body it is genuine; in the house it runs to surplus; in the village it lasts long; in the state it is ample; in all-under-heaven it is broad. Five stages, each carried into the next — Laozi's order of near-to-far, small-to-great. The Great Learning: "from the Son of Heaven down to the common man, all alike take the cultivation of the body as root" — the same architecture. And Laozi raised this frame before the Great Learning did: the inner unity of pre-Qin learning shows itself here.

Yet the spirit of the five ranks parts Confucian from Daoist. The Confucian pushes outward from the self: "extend and fill it"; the Daoist reaches things from the self — the self-so spreads of its own accord. The Confucian extends presence from presence; the Daoist lets absence cover absence. So the Great Learning says "extend oneself" where Laozi says 觀, "behold" — beholding is not extending: one's own De is held up as a mirror, and the De out there shows itself in it. By the body behold bodies, by the house houses, by the village villages, by the state states, by all-under-heaven all-under-heaven: verifying the outer by the inner, the far by the near, like lit by like. To know all-under-heaven, one state suffices for the proof; to know a state, one village suffices; to know a village, one house suffices; to know a house, one body suffices. This is the teaching of being near to the Dao.

Weightiest: the silk text reads 其德乃博, "its De grows broad," where Wang Bi puts 普, "universal." One graph, and the flavor parts. 博 is breadth of measure — abundance with room to spare; 普 is coverage — nothing left out. De spreads as rivers do, refusing no rivulet, as the sea declines no stream: wide of itself, everywhere without trying, so Laozi says 博. Wang Bi's 普 already leans toward the Confucian "extend it to all" — no longer Laozi's spreading-of-itself. The truth of the Dao lies in "taking the tending of the body as root, and governing state and house with what is left over": from the genuine to the broad, and the order must not be scrambled.

Last: "How do I know all-under-heaven is so? By this." What is "this"? The De of one's own body, nothing else. Knowing the world's order and disorder is no outward expedition but an inward verification. When the body's De is right, the house evens itself; the house even, the village concords of itself; the village concordant, the state orders itself; the state ordered, all-under-heaven levels itself. The sage knows all-under-heaven without stepping out the door, sees the Way of Heaven without peering through the window — the body for a mirror, De for the rule: Laozi's epistemology of politics at its most spare. The Doctrine of the Mean says "reach centered harmony, and heaven and earth take their places, the ten thousand things are nourished" — is this not the same word?
en.英譯:
What is well planted is not pulled up; what is well held does not slip away: sons and grandsons keep the sacrifice unbroken.

Cultivate it in the body, and its De (德) is genuine. Cultivate it in the house, and its De has surplus. Cultivate it in the village, and its De grows long. Cultivate it in the state, and its De grows ample. Cultivate it in all-under-heaven, and its De grows broad.

By the body, behold bodies; by the house, behold houses; by the village, behold villages; by the state, behold states; by all-under-heaven, behold all-under-heaven.

How do I know that all-under-heaven is so? By this.
